This is a REUSE.toml file, which is a standard metadata file used by the REUSE framework (https://reuse.software/) to declare licensing information for a software repository. All entries reference the standard 0BSD license (a permissive public-domain-like license) attributed to "Arch Linux contributors", which is entirely consistent with normal AUR packaging practices.

</details>

LLM auditresponse for new_version.sh:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard AUR maintainer helper script that automates the routine workflow of bumping a package to a new version. It downloads the upstream tarball from the project's own sourcehut repository (`https://git.sr.ht/~aeldit/aeosd/`), computes its SHA256 checksum, uses sed to update `pkgver=` and `sha256sums=` in the PKGBUILD, regenerates `.SRCINFO` via `makepkg --printsrcinfo`, and cleans up the downloaded file.

The downloaded tarball is never executed - it is only used to compute a checksum. `curl` is invoked with `--fail` so HTTP error pages won't be saved. All operations are confined to the package directory and serve the stated purpose of updating the package version. This matches the pattern of routine maintainer helper scripts (update.sh/bump.sh) described in the audit guidelines, and shows no signs of obfuscation, data exfiltration, backdoors, or execution of untrusted code.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard maintainer update script; downloads from own upstream and computes checksum only.</summary>
</security_assessment>

<details>
This is a standard PKGBUILD for a Rust-based screen brightness OSD application. The source tarball is fetched from the project's own sourcehut repository at a pinned version (0.4.0), and a sha256sum is provided for verification. The prepare() and build() functions use cargo's --locked and --frozen flags to ensure reproducible builds with locked dependency versions. The package() function installs a binary to /usr/bin and a udev rule to /etc/udev/rules.d/, which is normal for hardware-interacting applications. No malicious behavior is present: no unexpected network destinations, no obfuscated code, no data exfiltration, and no execution of untrusted content.
</details>
